subsection.title: The Cartesian Coordinate System
subsection.paragraph: In Section 1.1, we saw how a one-to-one correspondence between the set of real numbers and the points on a straight line leads to a coordinate system on a line (a one-dimensional space).

In a similar manner, we can represent points in a plane (a two-dimensional space) by using the Cartesian coordinate system , which we construct as follows: Take two perpendicular lines, one of which is normally chosen to be horizontal. These lines intersect at a point $$O$$ , called the origin (Figure 7). The horizontal line is called the $$\mathbf{x}$$ -axis, and the vertical line is called the $$\mathbf{y}$$ . A number scale is set up along the $$x$$ -axis, with the positive numbers lying to the right of the origin and the negative numbers lying to the left of it. Similarly, a number scale is set up along the $$y$$ -axis, with the positive numbers lying above the origin and the negative numbers lying below it.

figure.caption: The Cartesian coordinate system
figure.alt_text: A vertical perpendicular line intersects a horizontal line through point O, labeled Origin. The intersection lies near the center of both lines. The horizontal line is labeled x axis and the vertical line is labeled y axis.

subsection.paragraph: The number scales on the two axes need not be the same. Indeed, in many applications, different quantities are represented by $$x$$ and $$y$$ . For example, $$x$$ may represent the number of smartphones sold, and $$y$$ may represent the total revenue resulting from the sales. In such cases, it is often desirable to choose different number scales to represent the different quantities. Note, however, that the zeros of both number scales coincide at the origin of the two-dimensional coordinate system.

We can represent a point in the plane in this coordinate system by an ordered pair of numbers—that is, a pair $$(x,y)$$ , in which $$x$$ is the first number and $$y$$ is the second. To see this, let $$P$$ be any point in the plane (Figure 8). Draw perpendiculars from $$P$$ to the $$x$$ -axis and to the $$y$$ -axis. Then the number $$x$$ is precisely the number that corresponds to the point on the $$x$$ -axis at which the perpendicular line through $$P$$ crosses the $$x$$ -axis. Similarly, $$y$$ is the number that corresponds to the point on the $$y$$ -axis at which the perpendicular line through $$P$$ crosses the $$y$$ -axis.

figure.caption: An ordered pair ( x , y )
figure.alt_text: A point P is plotted on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis x and the vertical axis y intersect at point O near the bottom left corner of the viewing window. Point P (x, y) is plotted near the top right corner. A perpendicular is dropped from this point to each of the axes. The perpendicular to the x axis meets it at the mark x and the perpendicular to the y axis meets it at the mark y.

subsection.paragraph: Conversely, given an ordered pair $$(x,y)$$ with $$x$$ as the first number and $$y$$ the second, a point $$P$$ in the plane is uniquely determined as follows: Locate the point on the $$x$$ -axis represented by the number $$x$$ and draw a line through that point parallel to the $$y$$ -axis. Next, locate the point on the $$y$$ -axis represented by the number $$y$$ and draw a line through that point parallel to the $$x$$ -axis. The point of intersection of these two lines is the point $$P$$ (see Figure 8).

In the ordered pair $$(x,y)$$ , $$x$$ is called the abscissa, or $$\mathbf{x}$$ -coordinate; $$y$$ is called the ordinate, or $$\mathbf{y}$$ -coordinate; and $$x$$ and $$y$$ together are referred to as the coordinates of the point $$P$$ .

Letting $$P(a,b)$$ denote the point with $$x$$ -coordinate $$a$$ and $$y$$ -coordinate $$b$$ , we plot the points $$A(2,3)$$ , $$B( - 2,3)$$ , $$C( - 2, - 3)$$ , $$D(2, - 3)$$ , $$E(3,2)$$ , $$F(4,0)$$ , and $$G(0, - 5)$$ in Figure 9. The fact that, in general, $$P(x,y) \neq P(y,x)$$ is clearly illustrated by points A and E.

subsection.paragraph: The axes divide the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane into four quadrants. Quadrant I consists of the points $$P(x,y)$$ that satisfy $$x > 0$$ and $$y > 0$$ ; Quadrant II, the points $$P(x,y)$$ , where $$x < 0$$ and $$y > 0$$ ; Quadrant III, the points $$P(x,y)$$ , where $$x < 0$$ and $$y < 0$$ ; and Quadrant IV, the points $$P(x,y)$$ , where $$x > 0$$ and $$y < 0$$ (Figure 10).

figure.caption: The four quadrants in the Cartesian plane
figure.alt_text: An illustration shows the Cartesian plane divided into four quadrants by the intersection of horizontal axis x and vertical axis y at point O. The top right quadrant is labeled Quadrant One (+, +). The top left quadrant of the plane is labeled Quadrant Two (minus, +). The bottom left quadrant of the plane is labeled Quadrant Three (minus, minus). The bottom right quadrant of the plane is labeled Quadrant Four (+, minus).

subsection.title: The Distance Formula
subsection.paragraph: One immediate benefit that arises from using the Cartesian coordinate system is that the distance between any two points in the plane may be expressed solely in terms of their coordinates. Suppose, for example, that $$(x_{1},y_{1})$$ and $$(x_{2},y_{2})$$ are any two points in the plane (Figure 11).
